license.name: European Union copyright notice in the GDACS feeds: CC BY 4.0, reuse allowed with credit to GDACS
license.notes: Every item of the RSS feed carries "Copyright notice: European Union (CC BY 4.0), reuse is allowed, provided appropriate credit to GDACS is given." (the channel element itself says "public domain"). The GDACS terms-of-use page states no licence; it is a disclaimer: information is provided as is, alerts are automatic and must not be used for decision making without confirmation from official sources.

limitations: Alerts for earthquakes, tsunamis and tropical cyclones are produced automatically by models and are not reviewed by experts before publication; impact estimates carry large uncertainties.
The alert level estimates the likely need for international humanitarian assistance, not the physical size of the event; GDACS does not replace official national warnings.
Each event is shown at a single centroid point; cyclone tracks, flood extents and drought areas are not included.
The main feed lists only the earthquakes GDACS currently notifies (a small subset of all earthquakes); population exposure is available only for events present in that feed.
The 'current' flag is taken from GDACS as is and is occasionally inconsistent with the event text (e.g. long droughts).
sources.confidenceNotes: GDACS publishes no confidence value, so records carry none; the 'temporary' flag of preliminary events is kept as an attribute. Severity is derived by this application from the GDACS alert colour of the event: Green → minor (1), Orange → severe (3), Red → extreme (4); the colour itself is kept as the severity label.

retention.note: Events are kept for 30 days after they ended or were last listed as current (droughts: 90 days).

sources.attribution: NOAA's International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS), NOAA NCEI

license.name: NOAA NCEI open data – no licence or restriction stated on the product page; citation requested (doi:10.25921/82ty-9e16)
license.notes: The product page describes IBTrACS as global, open and publicly reviewed, and asks users to cite Knapp et al. (2010) and the dataset (Gahtan et al., doi:10.25921/82ty-9e16), or 'NOAA's International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) data, accessed on [date]'. The formal NCEI metadata record (use/access constraints) could not be retrieved when this adapter was written, so the classification rests on the product page and on NOAA's general open-data practice. Tracks originate from WMO regional centres and other agencies named in the data.

limitations: Tracks of recent storms are PROVISIONAL: they come from operational advisories (e.g. tcvitals, NHC working best track) and are replaced by reanalysed best tracks months later.
The file is refreshed about once a day, so the last fix can be up to a day or more behind the real storm.

Wind speeds from different agencies use different averaging periods (1-minute for U.S. agencies, 10-minute for most WMO centres) and are not strictly comparable; the adapter reports the WMO value when present and otherwise the U.S. agency value.
Positions between the 6-hourly agency fixes are interpolated by IBTrACS to 3-hourly resolution.
sources.confidenceNotes: IBTrACS gives no per-storm confidence value; provisional tracks are labelled as such in the attributes. Severity is derived by this application from the highest sustained wind along the track: below 34 kt minor, 34–63 kt moderate, 64–95 kt severe, 96 kt and above extreme.

retention.note: A track is kept while the storm is in the ACTIVE list (7 days after its last fix) and for 30 days after its last fix.

coverage.temporal: Events with a dated position in the past 30 days (open or closed) plus every still-open volcano, iceberg and storm event regardless of age.

sources.attribution: NASA Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker (EONET)

license.name: NASA open data (no licence restriction stated; NASA asks to be acknowledged) – EONET disclaimer applies
license.notes: NASA ESDIS data-use guidance: data from NASA-led missions carry no use restrictions unless marked otherwise (CC0); citation is strongly urged. EONET disclaimer (https://eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov/what-is-eonet): metadata are for visualisation and general information only and are not 'official' with regard to spatial or temporal extent. Each event links to a third-party source whose own terms govern the linked material.

limitations: EONET positions and dates are approximations taken from the linked sources; the 'closed' date does not necessarily mark the real end of an event.
Many events are never closed upstream (thousands of old wildfire events remain 'open'), so open wildfires and other events without a dated position in the past 30 days are not fetched.
Volcano events usually carry only the date on which EONET first registered the activity, which can be years old for long-lived eruptions.
Storm positions are a few fixes per day from JTWC/NHC advisories; the line between them is drawn by this application and is not an analysed best track.
Flood events from GDACS are small circular/outline polygons around a reported location, not mapped flood extents.
sources.confidenceNotes: EONET gives no confidence or quality value, so records carry none. Severity is derived by this application for tropical cyclones only, from the peak sustained wind reported along the track (<34 kt minor, 34–63 kt moderate, 64–95 kt severe, 96 kt and above extreme); other event types have no severity.

retention.note: Events are kept while EONET lists them and for 30 days after they are closed or disappear from the feed (volcano events: 60 days).

license.notes: EULA as read on 2026-11-10: the licence covers non-commercial use; anything disclosed externally must be transformative and must not allow the dataset to be reverse engineered – "It is not sufficient for Licensed Content to simply be supplemented, appended, excerpted, reorganized, or made available through the Licensee's own dashboard." Governmental and some other organisations need additional authorisation. This source is therefore disabled by default and intended only for the account holder's own internal analysis on a non-public instance; do not enable it on a deployment that other people can reach. The bundled fixture is synthetic, not ACLED data.

limitations: Events are coded by researchers from media, NGO and local-partner reports; coverage and detail vary by country and are revised after publication.
Fatality numbers are the most conservative reported estimates and are frequently unverifiable.
Dates are whole days; locations are coded to a named place with a precision code (exact place, nearby area, or wider region).
Data are published weekly, so the most recent days are incomplete.
sources.confidenceNotes: Confidence is derived by this application from ACLED's geo-precision code only (1 exact location → 0.8, 2 near/within area → 0.6, 3 wider region → 0.4). It describes how precisely the event is located, not whether the report is true. Severity is derived from the reported fatality estimate.

retention.note: Events are kept for 60 days after they occurred, then purged; the EULA requires deleting ACLED data when the licence ends (delete the database file).

fixture.notes: lastupdate.txt is the live file as captured (its size/md5 columns describe the original 99 KB export, not the trimmed fixture). The export zip was built from seven real GDELT 2.0 15-minute export files captured from data.gdeltproject.org (20261107100000, 20261108160000, 20261109140000, 20261109210000, 20261110060000, 20261110120000 and 20261110174500): 460 real rows were selected (all usable protest rows, a place-diverse sample of conflict and cooperation rows, same-article duplicate codings, plus non-matching rows: country-level geocodes, verbal events, low-mention cooperation and retrospective SQLDATEs), concatenated in time order with each row keeping its own DATEADDED, and re-zipped with fflate under the newest file's name so that the real unzip path is exercised. Two privacy trims were applied to every row: the unused Actor1Name/Actor2Name columns were blanked, and SOURCEURL was reduced to the publisher's origin plus a '#gdelt-fixture-<hash>' fragment (article slugs can carry names of individuals); all other columns are unmodified. The malformed variant is a hand-authored 15-row export (zipped the same way) using example.org URLs.

sources.dataset: GDELT 2.0 Event Database – 15-minute event export
sources.description: Machine-coded events (CAMEO taxonomy) extracted automatically from worldwide news reports: material conflict, protests and diplomatic/material cooperation, geocoded by GDELT to the city or landmark named in the text.

coverage.geographic: Global, wherever monitored news media report; strongly skewed towards countries and cities with dense (English-language and translated) media coverage.
coverage.temporal: Only the most recent 15-minute export is read on each poll; events are kept locally for 14 days.

updateCadence.upstream: A new export file every 15 minutes

sources.attribution: The GDELT Project (https://www.gdeltproject.org/)

license.name: GDELT Terms of Use – unrestricted use and redistribution with citation and link
license.notes: "All datasets released by the GDELT Project are available for unlimited and unrestricted use for any academic, commercial, or governmental use of any kind without fee"; redistribution is permitted provided a citation to the GDELT Project and a link to gdeltproject.org are included. Linked news articles remain the copyright of their publishers; only the article URL is stored.

limitations: Events are produced by fully automated text coding of news reports. They are NOT verified: false positives, mis-attributed actors, metaphorical language coded as violence and duplicates of one incident are common.

The location is GDELT's machine geocode of a place name found in the article; it can be the place where something was said or reported rather than where it happened. Only city/landmark-level matches (ActionGeo_Type 3 or 4) are shown; country- and state-level matches are dropped because they pile up on centroids.

The event time shown is DATEADDED (when GDELT first saw the report, 15-minute resolution, UTC), not the time of the underlying incident. Rows whose coded event day (SQLDATE) lies more than 2 days before DATEADDED – retrospective mentions such as anniversaries – are skipped.
Counts of mentions, sources and articles cover only the first 15 minutes after the event was first seen and are never updated.
Cooperation events are kept only when NumMentions is at least 3; rows coded from the same article with the same CAMEO root code at the same place are collapsed into one record.
Only the newest export file is fetched per poll: if the application is down or a poll is missed, the intermediate 15-minute files are not back-filled.
Coverage reflects media attention, not the true distribution of events.
sources.confidenceNotes: GDELT is an automated machine-coding system, not a curated event dataset: every record is a claim that some news report was algorithmically read as describing this type of event at this place. Confidence is derived by this application and deliberately low: 0.20 for a single source, plus 0.05 per additional source seen in the first 15 minutes, capped at 0.50. No severity is assigned. Titles are generated from the CAMEO event-type label and the geocoded place name and are prefixed with "Media-reported".

retention.note: Events are kept for 14 days after DATEADDED, then purged.

layers.name: Media-reported conflict (GDELT)
layers.description: Machine-coded 'material conflict' events from news reports (CAMEO 15–20: force posture, reduced relations, coercion, assault, fighting, mass violence). Unverified; city-level machine geocode.

layers.name: Media-reported protests (GDELT)
layers.description: Machine-coded protest events from news reports (CAMEO 14: demonstrations, strikes, blockades, riots). Unverified; city-level machine geocode.

layers.name: Media-reported diplomacy & cooperation (GDELT)
layers.description: Machine-coded cooperation events from news reports (CAMEO 03–08: intent to cooperate, consultations and visits, diplomatic and material cooperation, aid, concessions) with at least 3 mentions. Unverified.

sources.dataset: Live aircraft state vectors (REST API /states/all)
sources.description: Current ADS-B / Mode S state vectors of airborne aircraft received by the volunteer OpenSky sensor network: position, altitude, velocity, track, vertical rate, squawk and callsign exactly as broadcast.

envVars.name: OPENSKY_CLIENT_ID
envVars.description: client_id of an OpenSky API client (OAuth2 client-credentials flow). Optional: without it the anonymous quota applies.

envVars.name: OPENSKY_CLIENT_SECRET
envVars.description: client_secret belonging to OPENSKY_CLIENT_ID. Both must be set for authenticated requests.

auth.setup: IMPORTANT: OpenSky's terms require a prior written agreement for any operational use of the REST API (integration into a live product, service or automated system, even internal and even for non-profit or government users) and a written licence for any commercial entity. Obtain that agreement first (contact@opensky-network.org); this source is therefore disabled by default. Credentials are optional: log in to your OpenSky account, open the Account page, create an API client and set OPENSKY_CLIENT_ID and OPENSKY_CLIENT_SECRET. The adapter exchanges them for a 30-minute Bearer token at auth.opensky-network.org. Without credentials the anonymous quota (400 credits/day, 4 credits per global query) applies, which is what the 15-minute poll interval is sized for. Do not register multiple accounts.

sources.attribution: The OpenSky Network, https://opensky-network.org – Schäfer, Strohmeier, Lenders, Martinovic, Wilhelm: "Bringing up OpenSky: A large-scale ADS-B sensor network for research", ACM/IEEE IPSN 2014

license.name: OpenSky Network General Terms of Use & Data License Agreement – non-profit research and education only; written licence required for operational or commercial use
license.notes: Terms as read on 2026-11-10 (copy archived 2026-10-14): the licence is limited to non-profit research and non-profit education. Any use by a for-profit or commercial entity, and any operational use of the REST API in a live product, service or automated system (even internal, even non-profit or governmental), requires a previous written agreement with OpenSky Network. The data may not be distributed or made available to third parties (section 3.iii); publications must cite the IPSN 2014 paper and de-identify aircraft identifiers (sections 3.i, 4.i); copies must be expunged when the research ends. For these reasons this source ships disabled and its bundled fixture is synthetic, not captured OpenSky data.

limitations: Licence: running this adapter in a deployed, automatically polling system is 'operational use' under OpenSky's terms and needs a prior written agreement; without one, use is limited to non-profit research and education and data must not be passed on to third parties.

Crowd-sourced receiver coverage: aircraft outside receiver range (oceans, remote regions) and aircraft without ADS-B/Mode S transponders are simply absent – absence is not evidence that no aircraft is there.
The REST API carries no MLAT positions; some military, government and privacy-flagged aircraft are not distributed by the network.
Anonymous quota is 400 credits per day and a global query costs 4, so positions are refreshed only every 15 minutes: the map shows a sparse snapshot, not a continuous track.
OpenSky may block requests from cloud/hyperscaler IP ranges.

Callsign, squawk and altitude are self-reported by the transponder and can be wrong or deliberately misleading; 'originCountry' is only the state that allocated the ICAO 24-bit address block, not the operator's nationality or the aircraft's location.
sources.confidenceNotes: No per-record confidence is published. Positions are transponder self-reports relayed by volunteer receivers without independent verification. Severity 3 is assigned by this application only to the emergency transponder codes 7500, 7600 and 7700 as broadcast; such codes are frequently set by mistake.

retention.note: Only the latest position per aircraft plus the short recent path are kept; observations are purged after 1 day, in line with OpenSky's requirement not to retain data longer than needed.

sources.description: CISA's authoritative catalog of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with reliable evidence of active exploitation in the wild, with remediation due dates for US federal agencies and a ransomware-use flag.

coverage.geographic: Not geographic: global security bulletins about software and hardware products.
coverage.temporal: Catalog entries since 2021-11-03; this application keeps entries added during the last 90 days.

updateCadence.upstream: Republished whenever CISA adds or amends entries, typically several times per week on US business days.

license.name: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal
license.notes: CISA's licence file states: "The KEV database is distributed under the Creative Commons 0 1.0 License. You may use this data in any legal manner but note that information provided at any 3rd party links included in the KEV database are bound by the policies and licenses of those 3rd party websites. Use of the information does not authorize you to use the CISA Logo or DHS Seal, nor should such use be interpreted as an endorsement by CISA or DHS."

limitations: The catalog is not a list of all exploited vulnerabilities: an entry requires an assigned CVE ID, reliable evidence of active exploitation and clear remediation guidance, so inclusion can lag first exploitation by days to years.

dateAdded is a calendar date without a time; it is placed at 00:00 UTC of that day. It is the date CISA added the entry, not the date of first exploitation or disclosure.

knownRansomwareCampaignUse 'Unknown' means CISA lacks confirmation, not that ransomware use has been ruled out.
Only entries added in the last 90 days are ingested; entries that CISA removes from the catalog (rare) remain visible here until retention expires.
sources.confidenceNotes: CISA publishes no per-entry confidence, so confidence is left empty. Inclusion itself reflects CISA's assessment that there is reliable evidence of active exploitation. Severity is derived by this application, not published by CISA: 4 (extreme) when knownRansomwareCampaignUse is 'Known', otherwise 3 (severe) because every catalog entry is actively exploited; it is not a CVSS score.

retention.note: Entries are ingested while they are at most 90 days old (by dateAdded) and purged 120 days after dateAdded.

sources.provider: IODA – Internet Outage Detection and Analysis (Internet Intelligence Lab, Georgia Institute of Technology)
sources.dataset: IODA HTTP API v2 – country-level outage events
sources.description: Automatically detected drops in country-level Internet connectivity signals (BGP-visible /24 blocks, active probing, network-telescope traffic). Each event is a possible outage signal from one data source with a start, a duration and a severity score; it is not a confirmed outage or shutdown.

coverage.geographic: Global, country level (IODA also publishes sub-national region and AS-level events, which are not ingested).
coverage.temporal: Events active during the past 7 days, including events that started up to 14 days before that window and were still active in it.

updateCadence.upstream: Signals are evaluated continuously (BGP visibility every 5 minutes, active probing of each /24 block at least every 10 minutes); events appear and grow with a lag of minutes to a few hours

sources.attribution: IODA, Internet Intelligence Lab, Georgia Institute of Technology

license.name: No data licence or terms of use published (public research API)
license.notes: As of 2026-11-10 neither the IODA dashboard (home, help, about/acknowledgements pages), nor the API documentation states a licence, terms of use or citation requirement for the data; the API is public and needs no key. The IODA software (github.com/InetIntel/ioda-api, ioda-ui) is released by the Regents of the University of California for academic research and education purposes only, which covers the code, not the data. Because no reuse terms are published, redistribution is recorded as unknown and the source is conservatively flagged non-commercial; credit IODA / Georgia Tech and contact ioda-info@cc.gatech.edu before any commercial or bulk reuse.

limitations: Events are produced by automated change detection on aggregate signals: IODA raises an alert when a signal falls below a fraction of the median of a sliding window of recent values. A drop can be caused by measurement artefacts, routing changes, maintenance or geolocation changes as well as by a real outage; IODA describes itself as an operational prototype.

Each record is one event from one data source (bgp, ping-slash24 or merit-nt). The same incident seen by several sources appears as several records for the same country; agreement between sources is expressed in the confidence value.
Events detected with the experimental SARIMA method (currently the Google Transparency Report signal) are excluded with ignoreMethods=*.sarima, as IODA's own dashboard does.
For an event that is still active, the API clips the duration at the query time and the score keeps growing; start times of long-running events can also be revised when IODA re-segments its alerts.

Country attribution relies on IP geolocation of address blocks. Small countries and territories with few routed /24 blocks produce frequent low-magnitude events. Territories absent from this application's country gazetteer (e.g. Gibraltar, Guadeloupe, Réunion, Tokelau) are not shown.
The severity level and the mean relative drop are derived by this application from IODA's score and duration; they are not IODA classifications.
sources.confidenceNotes: IODA measures drops in three independent connectivity signals per country: BGP (number of /24 blocks visible to more than 50 % of full-feed Route Views / RIPE RIS peers), active probing (number of /24 blocks responding to Trinocular-style pings) and a network telescope (unique source IPs seen at the Merit darknet). The upstream score is IODA's 'alert area': relative drop in percent multiplied by the outage length in minutes. Confidence is derived by this application from how many of these data sources report overlapping events for the same country (IODA: 'we use multiple datasources to gain confidence about an outage'): one source 0.4, two 0.65, three or more 0.85. Severity is derived from the mean relative drop (score ÷ minutes) and the duration: extreme ≥ 70 % for ≥ 3 h, severe ≥ 40 % for ≥ 1 h, moderate ≥ 10 % for ≥ 30 min, minor ≥ 2 %, otherwise info. These are possible outage signals, not confirmed outages or government-ordered shutdowns.

retention.note: Events are kept for 30 days after they ended, then purged. Events that IODA no longer lists (re-segmented or withdrawn) are closed by the pipeline.

fixture.notes: Both files were captured from the live services.swpc.noaa.gov on 2026-11-10. ovation_aurora_latest.json (920 KB, 65,160 cells) was trimmed to two contiguous latitude bands that contain both auroral ovals – 60°N…80°N and 88°S…48°S, all 360 longitudes, 22,320 cells, values untouched – and re-serialised compactly with the envelope (Observation Time, Forecast Time, Data Format, type) intact. Snapshot fixture: Observation Time was re-timed from 2026-11-10T17:43:00Z to 2026-11-10T23:52:00Z (eight minutes before the fixture epoch) and Forecast Time by the same offset from 18:26:00Z to 2026-11-11T00:35:00Z – the forecast's valid time is by nature 43 minutes after the observation and therefore falls after the epoch; the adapter uses the Observation Time as the record time. Geomagnetic activity was low at capture (maximum probability 21 %). alerts.json is the complete, unmodified capture (69 messages from 2026-10-11 to 2026-11-10 05:01 UTC, 21 of them within the 7 days before the epoch); no re-timing was needed. The two malformed variants were authored by hand.

coverage.temporal: Aurora: the latest 30–90 minute forecast. Alerts: messages issued during the last 7 days (the file itself holds about a month).

sources.attribution: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center

license.name: U.S. Government work – public domain (NOAA/NWS)
license.notes: The SWPC data-access page lists services.swpc.noaa.gov/json and /products as the public data service and states no separate licence; the site links to the NOAA/NWS disclaimer, under which NWS web information is in the public domain unless noted otherwise and must not be presented as official material after modification.

limitations: The aurora layer is a model forecast (OVATION Prime driven by solar-wind measurements at L1), not an observation of visible aurora; visibility also depends on darkness, cloud and local viewing conditions.

To keep the layer light, only grid cells with a probability of at least 10 % are kept and the grid is thinned to every second degree of longitude and latitude, so the mapped oval is a 2° sample of the 1° product.
Alerts are global bulletins with no geographic footprint; they are listed, not mapped. Only the title line and a short excerpt are stored – consult SWPC for the authoritative text.
The JSON products are operational files without a formal schema or stability guarantee.
sources.confidenceNotes: Neither product carries a confidence value, so none is assigned. Alert severity is derived by this application from the NOAA Space Weather Scale level (G/S/R 1–5) when the message states one: level 1 (Minor) → 1, 2 (Moderate) → 2, 3 (Strong) → 3, 4 (Severe) → 3, 5 (Extreme) → 4; messages without a scale level have no severity. Aurora cells carry the model probability as their metric and no severity.

retention.note: Aurora cells are updated in place and purged 1 day after their last forecast; alert bulletins are kept for 30 days.

Proximity to a plate boundary says nothing by itself about current seismic or volcanic hazard.

ShareAlike: adaptations of the data that are redistributed must carry the same licence. Only a short excerpt (at most 300 characters) of each description is stored; site images are not used.

limitations: One reference point per property: serial and transboundary properties (routes, groups of monuments, large parks) extend far beyond that point, and two serial properties are published without any coordinates and are attached to their State(s) Party instead.

The 'in danger' flag is the formal List of World Heritage in Danger decided by the Committee once a year; it is not a real-time damage or threat assessment, and sites under acute threat may not (yet) be listed.
The States listed are the States Parties that nominated the property, as published by UNESCO; this is not a statement about sovereignty (the Old City of Jerusalem is published without a State Party).
Open-data API quota: 10,000 requests per day per client; the dataset itself is refreshed about once a year.

retention.note: Reference data: a property is kept for as long as UNESCO lists it; delisted properties disappear with the next refresh.
